title: Theo and the Clock
premise: In the winter of 1917, battlefield nurse Elodie Sterling keeps a hidden ledger of the soldiers whose deaths the officers' reports omit — names measured against what can be carried when evacuation orders come. When the season's last bridge over the river closes and a wounded officer, Theo Marchand, arrives carrying proof that a 'victorious' engagement was a catastrophic blunder covered up by command, Elodie must smuggle both him and her ledger across enemy lines of bureaucracy to reach a war correspondent before the victors' historians seal the record. Betrayed by the chaplain she trusted and hunted by an intelligence captain who once loved her, she trades her own safe passage for the truth. The book ends at the reopened spring crossing: Theo survives to testify, the ledger enters the official record under both their names, and Elodie — stripped of her post but not her purpose — chooses belonging with Theo over the duty that would have erased them both.
about_author: Quentin Vasquez is the pen name of a former military archivist who spent a decade cataloguing field hospital records from the Great War before turning to fiction. He writes from a farmhouse in the Loire Valley, where he restores broken clocks that no longer need to tell the time.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In a flooded dressing station, Elodie records in her hidden ledger the men the morning report leaves out, weighing each name against the supplies she must abandon on the next evacuation order. Introduces her method, her cynicism about official paper, and her quiet grief. Emotional beat: the cost of remembering when forgetting is survival.

chapters.title: Orders Come at Dusk
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The evacuation order arrives; Elodie triages what can be carried — morphine, one stretcher per wagon, no records. She watches a dying sergeant's name go unrecorded and adds it to the ledger by candlelight. First mention that the river bridge will close for the season within weeks. Beat: duty as arithmetic, love as what refuses to be counted.

chapters.title: A Man Carried Out of the Mist
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Theo Marchand is brought in half-dead from a reconnaissance gone wrong, clutching a satchel he refuses to release even unconscious. As Elodie works to save him, she glimpses maps and a signed order inside. He wakes, mistakes her for a chaplain, and asks her to swear the satchel reaches Paris. Beat: the first crack in her detachment.

chapters.title: What the Satchel Holds
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, fevered and fragmented. Theo recalls the engagement at Virey Wood: the assault ordered anyway after scouts reported impossible ground, four hundred men spent to protect a colonel's reputation. His testimony was refused; his evidence nearly confiscated. He trusts no one — until the nurse who counts the uncounted. Beat: two keepers of forbidden records recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Chaplain's Kindness
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Father Aubert, the camp chaplain, offers to help move Theo and the documents, claiming contacts with church couriers to Paris. Elodie, exhausted, half-believes him; Theo warns her that kindness near command is a currency someone is spending. The bridge closure is moved up — ten days now. Beat: hope planted that will become betrayal.

chapters.title: Captain Hale Arrives
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Intelligence Captain Edmund Hale comes to the station investigating 'document irregularities.' He and Elodie share a history — a courtship ended by her enlistment — and he offers her protection in exchange for any papers passing through her ward. She lies to his face for the first time. Beat: old love weaponized into surveillance.

chapters.title: Ten Days to the Bridge
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A countdown chapter: Elodie hides the ledger inside a clock casing from the station chapel while planning Theo's transfer south. Small acts of resistance ripple through the nurses, who begin bringing her names unprompted. The station becomes a quiet conspiracy. Beat: belonging found in shared risk rather than shared orders.

chapters.title: The Clock That Kept More Than Time
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, recovering. Theo helps Elodie dismantle and reassemble the chapel clock around her ledger, and in the slow work they speak plainly — his guilt over the men he led, her fear that memory changes nothing. They admit, without saying it, that they are falling in love. Beat: tenderness inside a ticking deadline.

chapters.title: Aurelie's Crossing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A local ferrywoman, Aurelie, agrees to move Theo downriver past the closed bridge for a price Elodie cannot fully pay — her mother's ring and a favor owed later. The plan is set for the third night. Hale grows suspicious of the chapel. Beat: the machinery of escape clicking into place, too smoothly.

chapters.title: The Search of Ward Three
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Hale orders a search and finds nothing — because Father Aubert has already quietly tipped him off about the satchel while pretending to warn Elodie. Hale, torn between duty and feeling, lets the search come up empty but posts watchers on the road. Beat: the reader sees the trap closing before Elodie does.

chapters.title: Third Night
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The escape begins: Theo carried on a stretcher through fog to the riverbank, the ledger-clock left behind as decoy. At the bank, lanterns — Aubert has sold them. A soldier is shot; Elodie makes a split-second choice to draw the patrol toward herself so Theo can reach the water. Beat: sacrifice as the truest form of testimony.

chapters.title: Taken
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, in custody. Interrogated by Hale, she refuses to confirm anything, reciting casualty figures instead of answers. Hale reveals Aubert's betrayal and, worse, that the Virey Wood cover-up goes higher than a colonel — to a general writing the campaign history himself. Beat: fury transmuted into resolve; the stakes widen from a man to the record itself.

chapters.title: The Historian's Draft
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, hiding at Aurelie's mill downstream. Theo learns from a newspaper that General Vaillancourt's official account of Virey Wood is being serialized — heroes where there were corpses. With the bridge closed and Elodie captured, he must decide whether to run or return. Beat: despair, then the turn — he chooses her and the truth together.

chapters.title: What Hale Cannot File
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Ordered to transfer Elodie to divisional court, Hale reads her seized ledger pages — hundreds of names in her hand — and something breaks in him. He delays the transfer by one day, falsifying the escort schedule, unable to explain even to himself why. Beat: the antagonist's conscience becomes the story's hinge.

chapters.title: The Confession of Father Aubert
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Aubert visits her cell, unraveling: he informed not for ideology but because command threatened the orphanage he funds. Elodie, instead of cursing him, asks for one thing — a message passed to the mill. He agrees, weeping. Beat: mercy extended as strategy and grace at once.

chapters.title: Return Across the Water
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Guided back by Aurelie and armed with Aubert's message, Theo infiltrates the station during a bombardment alarm to reach Elodie — and finds Hale waiting, alone, holding her ledger. Instead of arresting him, Hale hands over the clock and says only: 'Make it count.' Beat: the climax's door opening.

chapters.title: The Correspondent at Chalon
chapters.summary: Shared POV, alternating. Elodie freed by Hale's forged orders, she and Theo race to Chalon where correspondent Marguerite Osei is filing the last dispatch before the press embargo seals the campaign narrative. They lay ledger beside testimony beside the original order — but Osei needs verification Hale could hang for providing. Beat: everything wagered on one transmission.

chapters.title: Ninety Minutes Before the Wire Closes
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The telegraph office, the countdown, Hale arriving with the authenticated order copy just ahead of Vaillancourt's adjutant. The dispatch goes out naming the dead of Virey Wood in full. The adjutant bursts in seconds too late. Beat: pure kinetic climax — the truth beating the historians by minutes.

chapters.title: Reckoning at Division
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Hale surrenders himself, accepting court-martial to shield Elodie and Theo; his testimony forces an inquiry into Virey Wood. Vaillancourt's history is suspended pending investigation. Elodie watches the man who hunted her choose justice outside every law that employed him. Beat: costly, unsentimental vindication.

chapters.title: The Bridge Opens
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Spring; the bridge reopens and the first convoy crosses. Elodie, dismissed from service for the affair, stands at the railing with her ledger — now entered into the inquiry record, every name read aloud in session. Theo joins her, walking stick in hand. Beat: grief and relief braided; the dead finally counted.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo and Elodie travel to Virey Wood itself, planting markers for the four hundred, and Theo finally writes his own account — not for command but for the families. Elodie begins a new ledger: not the omitted dead, but the living who helped. Beat: transformation of witness into inheritance.

chapters.title: Theo and the Clock
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, years later. In the Loire farmhouse, the chapel clock — repaired, its hollow now filled with letters instead of ledgers — chimes as their daughter asks about the names carved on the mantel. Elodie tells her the truth simply. Final line returns to the opening image: measure the world in what can be carried. Beat: peace earned, memory kept alive by love.
